content: The systematic reviews conducted for the update of the World Health Organization (WHO) Guideline on Country Pharmaceutical Pricing Policies were authored by a team of experts from the Utrecht Centre for Pharmaceutical Policy and Regulation at Utrecht University in the Netherlands, and the York Health Economics Consortium in the United Kingdom. The second edition of the WHO guideline aims to provide evidence-based recommendations to assist countries in managing pharmaceutical pricing policies effectively. The WHO guideline, first published in 2015, was based on evidence reviewed in 2010. Since then, the body of literature on the effects of various government pricing policies has grown significantly. The primary objective of the review was to evaluate the effects of ten pharmaceutical pricing policies, implemented individually or in combination, on outcomes such as price, volume, availability, and affordability of pharmaceutical products. The review also considered less quantifiable outcomes and contextual factors that may influence the implementation of these policies. Specific objectives included estimating the effect size of pricing policies, developing evidence profiles using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) framework, and identifying practical and contextual considerations based on qualitative evidence from country experiences. The report is structured into 13 sections, beginning with an introduction and background. A common bibliography and detailed appendices on search strategies and excluded studies are also included. The systematic reviews adhered to principles outlined in the Cochrane Handbook and guidance from the Centre for Reviews and Dissemination. The reviews addressed two overarching research questions: (1) Which pharmaceutical pricing policies are effective in managing prices, volume, availability, and affordability of pharmaceutical products? (2) What contextual factors and implementation strategies influence the effects of specific pricing policies? The review included studies comparing eligible interventions against other strategies or counterfactuals, such as historical comparisons. Single policies or combinations of policies were eligible for inclusion, provided they described a comparator or counterfactual. Studies without such comparisons were excluded. Key pricing policies examined include: 1. External Reference Pricing (ERP): This involves using the price of a pharmaceutical product in one or more countries as a benchmark for setting or negotiating prices in another country. 2. Internal Reference Pricing: This uses the prices of identical or similar medicines within a country to derive a reference price for reimbursement or pricing decisions. 3. Value-Based Pricing: Prices for new medicines are set based on their therapeutic value, often assessed through health technology assessments (HTAs). 4. Cost-Plus Pricing: Prices are determined by accounting for production costs, promotional expenses, research and development, administrative costs, overheads, and profit margins. 5. Mark-Up Regulation: This involves setting maximum price thresholds or mark-up percentages across the pharmaceutical supply chain to control costs. 6. Price Transparency: 7. Discounts for Single-Source Pharmaceuticals: Price reductions granted under specific conditions, such as managed-entry agreements or risk-sharing arrangements. 8. Promotion of Generics and Biosimilars: 9. Tendering and Negotiation: Competitive procurement processes to determine prices for medicines based on quality, supply conditions, and other factors. 10. Tax Exemptions or Reductions: Policies to reduce or eliminate taxes on pharmaceuticals to improve affordability. The search strategy for the review was comprehensive, covering multiple databases and resources, and included studies published from 2004 onward. The search was not restricted by language, and non-English search terms and results were translated where necessary. The eligibility criteria focused on studies reporting primary outcomes such as price, volume, availability, and affordability, as well as secondary outcomes like transparency, system efficiencies, and adverse outcomes (e.g., shortages, quality issues, safety concerns, unethical conduct). The review also considered contextual factors and implementation strategies that could influence the effectiveness of pricing policies. The findings of this systematic review aim to provide updated evidence to inform WHO’s recommendations on pharmaceutical pricing policies, supporting countries in ensuring the affordability and accessibility of essential medicines.
